content: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a genetic condition inherited in an autosomal-dominant manner. The primary treatment for HCM typically involves the use of negative inotropic agents. However, observational studies and small randomized trials have suggested that pacing may provide symptomatic and functional benefits in certain patients. Several theories have been proposed to explain the potential benefits of pacing in HCM. While pacing is not considered a first-line treatment for HCM, it may be beneficial for patients who have relative or absolute contraindications to surgical interventions or alcohol septal ablation. Although randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted to compare pacing with other therapeutic options, no comprehensive Cochrane-style systematic review has been performed to date. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of pacing in patients with HCM who are either refractory to drug therapy or intolerant to it. A systematic search was conducted on April 14, 2010, across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Web of Science, without language restrictions. The inclusion criteria were RCTs with either parallel or crossover designs that assessed the benefits and harms of pacing in HCM. For crossover studies, only data from the first phase were considered. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors, and the risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane Handbook guidelines. Relative risks were calculated for dichotomous data, and mean differences were calculated for continuous data. Meta-analysis was performed when appropriate, and a narrative synthesis was provided when meta-analysis was not feasible. A QUORUM flow chart was used to document the study selection process. Five studies, reported in 10 papers, were identified. However, three of these studies provided data that were not usable, leaving only two studies (reported in seven papers) with a total of 105 participants for inclusion in the review. The available data were insufficient to assess outcomes such as all-cause mortality, cost-effectiveness, exercise capacity, quality of life, and peak oxygen consumption. In one study comparing active pacing to placebo pacing, exercise time decreased from 13.1 ± 4.4 minutes to 12.6 ± 4.3 minutes in the placebo group, while it increased from 12.1 ± 5.6 minutes to 12.9 ± 4.2 minutes in the active pacing group. The mean difference (MD) was 0.30 minutes, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of -1.54 to 2.14, which was not statistically significant. However, the same study demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. In the placebo group, LVOT obstruction decreased from 71 ± 32 mmHg to 52 ± 34 mmHg, while in the active pacing group, it decreased from 70 ± 24 mmHg to 33 ± 27 mmHg (MD -19.00 mmHg; 95% CI -32.29 to -5.71). Additionally, the New York Heart Association (NYHA) functional class improved in both groups, with a decrease from 2.5 ± 0.5 to 2.2 ± 0.6 in the placebo group and from 2.6 ± 0.5 to 1.7 ± 0.7 in the active pacing group (MD -0.50; 95% CI -0.78 to -0.22). When comparing active pacing to transcoronary ablation of septal hypertrophy (TASH), one study reported that the NYHA functional class improved from 3.2 ± 0.7 to 1.5 ± 0.5 in the TASH group and from 3.0 ± 0.1 to 1.9 ± 0.6 in the pacing group. However, left ventricular (LV) wall thickness remained unchanged in the pacing group, whereas it decreased from 22 ± 4 mm to 17 ± 3 mm in the TASH group (MD 0.60 mm; 95% CI -5.65 to 6.85). LVOT obstruction also decreased in both groups, from 80 ± 35.5 mmHg in the TASH group to 49.3 ± 37.7 mmHg in the pacing group. The authors concluded that the trials conducted to date lack sufficient information on clinically relevant endpoints. The existing data are derived from small studies with a high risk of bias, focusing primarily on physiological measures rather than meaningful clinical outcomes. The results are inconclusive, and further large, high-quality trials with more appropriate outcome measures are needed.
